items.title: How to Argue in the Trump Era Without Losing Your Mind
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his reaction to the shooting at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Ontario on Yom Kippur. David discusses the rise of violence against Jews around the world, and why condemnations of anti-Semitic violence ring hollow when they come from people who spread myths about Jewish conspiracies. Then, David is joined by Jessica Tarlov, the co-host of The Five on Fox News and the Raging Moderates podcast. They talk about her new book, I Disagree: Winning Arguments Without Losing Friends , and how her upbringing helped shape her ability to disagree cordially. David and Jessica also discuss when to debate someone versus when to ignore them so as not to give them a platform. Finally, David ends the show with a review of the novel Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be Jessica Tarlov, co-host of the Fox News program The Five and author of the new book I Disagree: Winning Arguments Without Losing Friends. She’s also the co-host with Scott Galloway of the Raging Moderates podcast. The book for discussion this week will be a much-acclaimed new novel, Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke, and I’ll be discussing that at the bottom of the program. But before either my dialogue with Jessica Tarlov or the book discussion of Yesteryear , I wanna open with some thoughts about an outrage that happened in a place very close to me, just this, these past days. On the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, the most holy day of the Jewish year, a gunman opened fire on the synagogue in this Canadian town, the Ontario town of Belleville. Many of the details of this incident remain a little murky, but what we do have is: The alleged gunman, the apparent gunman, is in hospital, and so is a police officer who gallantly came to the rescue of the synagogue. None of the worshippers in the synagogue were injured. The alleged gunman apparently used a shotgun, which discharged a lot of pellets, did a lot of physical damage, but it was not the kind of high-powered rifle that would’ve shot up this building. And so the people inside were safe. This story has become a big story in Ontario, in Canada, and around the world. It is one of a many of a long series of incidents of intensifying violence against Jewish worshippers all around the world since October 7th of 2023. To read about it in Belleville is very striking, however, and not just because it’s so close to me. I have worshipped at the synagogue, Sons of Jacob Synagogue, where the crime took place. I’ve spent a lot of time there. It’s near where I live in Ontario. I see this street in my mind, and it’s such a powerful symbol of how life has changed for North American Jews. The Sons of Jacob Synagogue is a congregation that dates back to the early 20th century, but the building was built in the middle 1950s. It’s a piece of modernist architecture, quite small, and it faces directly on a road in a residential neighborhood. There are no security precautions other than a locked door, because it was built at a time when it never occurred to the Jews of North America that they could face violence from their neighbors. That kind of threat was something they remembered, but from across the ocean and from a different time, not here and not now. But, of course, it is here, and it is now. And it is striking all over the continent, all over the world. When these kinds of incidents happen, a certain kind of speaker, a certain kind of politician, a certain kind of online influencer, a certain kind of journalist will say, It is very important not to conflate the Jews of here— wherever “here” is, Ontario and Canada, the United States, New York, wherever it is— with the Jews over there. We should not be blaming the Jews of Belleville for the crimes of the state of Israel. Now this kind of remark is intended to be a defense of the Jewish community that is under attack, but it is, in its own way, a form of incitement. Because when you say we must not conflate the Jews here with the Jews there, we must not blame our Jews for those Jews, what you’re doing is suggesting that there are some Jews who deserve the kind of violence just that happened. And what you’re also doing is offering safety to certain Jews on condition that they disavow others. We see a lot of this in remarks by some people who are disaffiliated Jews, who will say, We can be safer if only we separate ourselves from the Jews in Israel who are under attack. We can buy some safety for ourselves. I hear that, and I think that that is the counsel of cowardice. To buy safety for yourself by abandoning others, by separating yourself from others who equally deserve safety, that seems to me a reprehensible thing. But as a strictly factual matter, it’s just wrong. That the no-conflation argument— Don’t attack the Jews here for what the Jews over there did —begins with the foundation upon a lie. And the lie is the lie that we are hearing again and again that Israel committed genocide, that is, Nazi-like atrocities, in its war of self-defense that began when it was attacked so atrociously on October 7th, 2023. I once made it a project to dig back through the archives to find who was the first person who compared the state of Israel to the Nazis, and when did it happen? And as best I can tell, the first, or the first prominent person, to do it was the British historian Arnold Toynbee, who makes the point in a book published in 1954, the eighth volume of his Study of History. Within six years of the independence of the state of Israel, Arnold Toynbee is publishing a comparison of the state of Israel to the Nazis. Now, what makes the comparison extra piquant is that Arnold Toynbee was pretty Nazi-adjacent himself. He had been invited to meet with Adolf Hitler in 1936. He took the meeting, and he came back from the meeting praising Hitler’s good intentions and recommending that the British government find a way to learn to live in peace with Adolf Hitler, who wanted nothing more than a better deal for Germany and Europe. So the tradition is Israel is accused of being a Nazi state from the very beginning, by someone who is kind of Nazi-adjacent. And this is a pattern that I think many people who are involved in Jewish life have noticed never ceasing to stop. Because for so many people, what a convenience, what a mercy, what a gift it would be if only we could prove that the Jews were the real Nazis. What a relief. What a burden discharged. There’s a joke, I’m sure you’ve heard it, that the Germans will never forgive the Jews for Auschwitz. I’m happy to report in the modern state of Germany, which is a state that is, in fact, where friendship with Israel is a principle of the organization of the state, the Germans have forgiven the Jews for Auschwitz. But around the rest of the world, lots of people haven’t. Auschwitz is the ultimate nightmare reflection of modern civilization, and specifically of Western civilization and of the Christian culture on which that Western civilization was built. Auschwitz invites a burden of reflection and of guilt that understandably people chafe at. And the way to escape that burden of guilt for many people is to transfer it and to say, The people who are victims there, they deserved it in some way. They’re the culprits, or they deserve it now. Maybe they didn’t deserve it then, but they deserve it now. And so while Germany has forgiven the Jews for Auschwitz, the rest of the world is angrier than ever at the Jews for Auschwitz and so wants to make Auschwitz not just a thing the Jews suffered, but a thing the Jews did. And sad to report, there are Jews or people of Jewish origin who play this game by identifying themselves with the Jewish people and the Jewish community only in order to act as fellow accusers of the Jewish community and the Jewish people. A Democratic nominee for Congress, Brad Lander, who did an event on Yom Kippur where he accused the Jews of the state of Israel of genocide, and a man who’s always separated himself from the state of Israel when the state of Israel was in need, but is rushing to identify himself with the state of Israel when he can blame the state of Israel for Nazi-like crimes. In Canada, the place where the Belleville shooting took place, the leader of the small left-wing party, the New Democratic Party, is of Jewish origin, from a famous Jewish political dynasty in Canada. He opened the Yom Kippur holiday by again saying, as someone who separated himself from Israel always in its time of need, I will identify with Israel to accuse Israel . It’s a footnote to history here that I sometimes think about. The phrase blood libel refers to a myth that the Jews use blood in the making of matzah. And as far as historians can tell, the myth originated in England in the 1100s, when a boy disappeared and a local mob became convinced or was persuaded that the boy had been abducted by the local Jewish community and his blood used to make matzah, and then massacres then followed. This outrageously false accusation was recorded in a book written by a local monk who claimed to have been told that Jews did this by a man named Theobald of Cambridge, a converted Jew who revealed the secrets of the Jewish world, among them that Jews met once a year to pick a Christian child and condemn that child to death for his blood to be used in the making of matzah. Now, it’s not clear whether Theobald of Cambridge actually existed, or whether the monk who told the story invented him or distorted his words in some way. The history of Theobald of Cambridge is a little murky. I like to believe that he did exist. I like to believe that Theo—I like to imagine Theobald of Cambridge saying in the 1100s, As a Jew, I’m here to tell you that the Jews really do use blood in the making of matzah, and you’re right to go out and massacre them all to punish them for the crime I just invented to defame my own community. And what I want to say when I hear people saying, As a Jew, I accuse the Jews of being Nazis, is—we had one Theobald of Cambridge already. He did enough damage. We don’t need more. But the modern progressive left, whether its members are of Jewish origin or not, tends to identify the Jews as privileged and powerful, and therefore as dangerous. And they often will see the Holocaust itself not as a source of suffering and misery, of trauma, which continues to affect Jewish mentality and Jewish life all these years after it happened; they see the Holocaust as a source of Jewish power and privilege, and therefore something that needs to be redistributed from the Jews to someone who is more deserving, who needs their share of power and privilege, and the kind of power and privilege you get by having a Holocaust of your own. And that is what is going on with this conflation lie. The conflation to say, We are going to accuse the Jews of the very thing that was done to them. Of the thing that was done to them not only in the 1940s, but of the thing that was attempted against them on October 7th, 2023, when there was a Nazi-like atrocity against the Jews of Israel—mass murder, mass kidnapping, mass rape, mass torture. That was how this war started. And so to redistribute the odium for those offenses, we redistribute it to those who need to have the history of the Holocaust redistributed away from them. And that brings us to the shooting in Belleville. And whenever I make these points, which are very close to my heart, I’m asked the question, Well, are you saying that all criticism of the state of Israel must be anti-Semitic? Can’t somebody say things about the Jews and not be anti-Semitic? And obviously, that’s true. People do it all the time, including many Israelis. Israelis criticize their own state. But If you say, I want to criticize the Jews without being regarded as anti-Semitic, one of the great ways of criticizing the state of Israel without being anti-Semitic is not to be anti-Semitic. It’s not so hard. Not to have paranoid fantasies. Not to engage in ancient anti-Semitic tropes, not to deploy myths of Jewish conspiracy and secret power and privilege. Not, above all, to say, We are going to accuse the Jews of doing the thing that was done to them, because they don’t deserve the credit for it, and someone else needs it as a resource for their power and privilege. That is the path to the shooting in Belleville, Ontario, and to so many other crimes that we are seeing and suffering in our modern world. And now, my dialogue with Jessica Tarlov. [ Music ] Frum: If you’ve ever caught the program The Five on Fox News, and who hasn’t, you know exactly what Jessica Tarlov does for a living. She regularly sits down at a table with four people who disagree with her, and she does not flinch. Four against one, cameras rolling, millions watching, and somehow she walks away having made her point, without losing the room or her colleagues or her sense of humor about the whole thing. She’s fond of putting it simply: “I am outnumbered.” What most people don’t see is, was what led her there. In the same stretch of months that Jessica got engaged, got married, and became a mother, she also said goodbye to her father, who was fighting cancer. She learned he was dying while she was standing in her wedding dress, trying it on for the first time. He made it to the wedding anyway. She’s written about that year now in her first book, I Disagree: Winning Arguments Without Losing Friends, out this month. A fusion of memoir, political analysis, and cultural advice as to how all of us can be better citizens and better people. Tarlov is also co-host with Scott Galloway of the Raging Moderates podcast. Jessica, thanks for joining The David Frum Show. Jessica Tarlov: Thank you for having me. I’m so excited to be here. Frum: So you are quite a circumspect person in your public appearances, and this is a kind of a novel thing for you to be so open about your story. So for those who have not had a chance yet to open the book, tell us the story. Where does it begin, and where are you now? Tarlov: Well, it begins at my dining table growing up. The tale of Jessica Tarlov as you see her today begins around a boisterous, frantic table full of loud characters with different politics than the ones on The Five , but with a lot of personality and a lot of desire to engage and tussle with ideas. And one where equality was at the center of it all, i.e., my sister and I were always treated as an important element of the table, equal to others, with our seats that were ours no matter who was over for dinner that night, even big movie stars. And it really imbued this sense of, I’ve got something to say, and it’s worth your time, and I’m gonna make you listen to it. So that’s where it begins. Frum: Tell us about your father, your life with him, and your loss of him. Tarlov: So my dad was the coolest. He had this incredible career that went everywhere from being a speechwriter for Warren Berger to being an entertainment lawyer, then deciding he didn’t wanna do that anymore—that he wanted to produce movies and direct a few. Went into that. And his final career—when he passed away, he was a winemaker. So zigging and zagging all over the place. And he and my mother had an incredible love affair. And I write in the book about how even at the end when he passed away from tongue cancer—which he got from 9/11; we lived nearby to the towers—there was still romance to it. And he was just an enormous character in and of itself, but a really dedicated dad and someone who I think made it so clear to me that there were good paths to go on, and some not-so-good ones. And it doesn’t mean you don’t always go down the not-so-good ones, at least for a little bit. But that there’s this strong sense of right and wrong to things, of black and white. I guess a lot of lawyers feel that way. And that he wanted me to go out in the world and to try everything, even if it felt unorthodox. Frum: So you emphasize the disputatiousness of your family background. How disputatious was it? Tarlov: I mean, nothing violent. I think for your listeners, and it’ll make sense for you, like kind of normal Reform Jewish vibes, right? Working it all out all the time, and a lot of conversation. A lot of pushing and pulling. My parents, they would talk to us about their work problems. And my mom—she was a lawyer as well; they met as lawyers at Warner Brothers—and when she stopped working in law and she started writing, they became creative partners in basically everything that they did. So their work life was, in a lot of ways, the centerpiece of our discussions and our tables. So on the disputatious scale, certainly not a 10, but a good amount of friction, and my parents bringing their lives to the table for all of us to engage together. Frum: When did you become aware you had political views? Tarlov: 9/11 was a very seminal experience, I think, for all Americans, New Yorkers in particular. I spend a good amount of the book talking about this. What it was like to be evacuated. And then you come back, and seeing, which has really stuck with me, the flood of first responders from all over the country coming in, having fire trucks parked on your block with license plates from far-flung places, like Idaho. And that it really contextualized my life as part of the American experience, more than this New Yorker silo that I had been living in quite happily. Frum: But you’re on television to express clear, distinct, sharp points of view in a pointed way. When did all of that come into focus? Tarlov: I don’t think until I started actually going on TV and doing it, and maybe not even until I got my regular co-hosting role on The Five, which is about four and a half years ago now. And I’ve been a contributor at Fox for a little bit less than 10 years in total. And you do TV segments regularly, so you know that when you kind of dip in and out, it’s very different than "this is your job,” and you’re thinking about it all the time. And you’re building your arguments throughout the course of the entire day, which is essentially how I see my life. From the morning I wake up, until I go to bed, I’m thinking about building these arguments, and how I’m processing whatever’s going on in our political landscape, and how I can make a solid argument about it that I could get out in 30 seconds if I’m gonna be interrupted, which is what happens regularly on The Five. So I think it’s a new thing for me. But having a background in research and political polling, I was already thinking about the best formulation for a particular sentiment anyway, because that’s the kind of question that you wanna go out into the field to ask people, right? To find out how it is that they think about, or what it is that they think about X, Y, or Z issue. Frum: Well, I’ll just say personally, since you mentioned it, I don’t actually do television all that often. I used to do it more. I’ve really dialed it back. And among the reasons I’ve dialed it back is—and I upset bookers—a booker will call me and say, Will you come on? And I’ll say, I haven’t thought about it, or, I don’t have a strong view on that subject. Or worst of all— Tarlov: Oh, they hate that. Frum: I don’t know enough. I remember a booker once said to me—I said, I don’t know enough about the subject. And she said, If people took that view, television would cease to exist. But do you feel like you’re cast into a role? Are you able to express what you think, or is there something that the drama that you’re a part of needs you to do, and therefore you are called upon to do it? Tarlov: I don’t like to be guided by the drama. I sit in the liberal seat on The Five. It is one against four. If I don’t say it, nobody else is going to. I mean, there are rare moments where there’s a good amount of consensus, or somebody takes a contrarian view, like on tariffs, for instance. So obviously someone like Dana Perino, who you know, is going to talk about the reality of what tariffs are, and that they’re a tax on the consumer, and it’s going to be passed down to us, et cetera. But in general, I am the one who is going to be taking the contrarian position. It does make it when I either agree with the others—or have a position that might not be certainly the Republican or the MAGA position, but isn’t necessarily the position of Democratic leadership—it would stick out then. If we’re talking about sometimes around immigration, for instance. Where I think that I was tacking, I don’t want to say to the right, but was certainly very hyper-aware of how open our border was in I’d say year three, really, of the Biden administration. And then the changes that he put in place to clamp down on it in his last year, and then obviously what’s happened since Donald Trump came in. But in general, yeah; it’s me. Frum: Let me ask you about the analytic part of your book and how you engage in, as you call it, storytelling, or disputation, or whatever you do on television. I don’t know how seriously to take the social science, but there’s a lot of social science that purports to claim that Americans are—as individuals and as groups within the national polity—more divided from one another than they were before. So in a world in which people, it seems, are more hostile to one another, or Americans are more hostile to one another than they were before, how do you do what you do? And what do you think you’re doing? Tarlov: What do I think I’m doing? So obviously I’ve seen all of those studies. I used to focus on specifically Gen Zs and Millennials. I was the head of research at a big women’s digital lifestyle publication. And so I would do surveys, quantitative and qualitative, of young Americans. And that trend line is very much real—that young people don’t want to date others with a different political point of view, or party affiliation, because for them it’s about morality. And I think that that’s actually core to the way people are reacting even to the subtitle of my book. Which I knew I was going to get, because it’s I Disagree: Winning Arguments Without Losing Friends , and a lot of people are very happy to lose those friends. This is usually liberals who feel like Trumpism is a moral stain, and that if you don’t share the same kind of values with people, why do you really need to be having a conversation, let alone sharing a Thanksgiving table? If you can get past the idea that you should just be nice to people because you’re blood related. So I do think that those trend lines are real. But I think that they also do not capture something that is also very real, which is our desire to continue to be in each other’s lives. But one of the main reasons that I wrote this book, and it was really two-pronged, but one of them is that I hear from viewers of all political stripes. So we have about 3.5 to 4 million viewers on a daily basis. Half are Republicans, so that’s MAGA to Romney Republicans. Then 30 percent independents, and about 20 percent Democrats. So a real spectrum of people are tuning into The Five, and that doesn’t even mention the folks that see clips of it that are all over the internet. But people were reaching out, and continue to, where they just say, How do you do it? I don’t know how you can do this. And these are folks who love Jesse Watters and people who detest Jesse Watters. And the people who want to know how I do it want to also know how they can do it, too. And you see this in focus groups a lot as well, that you talk to people especially. I’ve listened to a lot of them through Sarah Longwell, and in other venues. You listen to these swing-state voters where their vote actually matters. I don’t have that. You know, I vote in New York City, so we’re denominations of blue. But there is a lot of sadness in people’s stories and in their voices when they’re talking about the relationships that they have lost. And that the politics matters, but what matters more is finding a way to be able to communicate the politics and keep the relationships. That there has to be a way where we can do that. Frum: Okay, so give us the action plan. How do we do it? Our anti-vax uncle has been invited to Thanksgiving one more time. How are we to do it? Tarlov: So, some of my answer I think will be very hard for people when you are talking to people whose views are so aggravating and run so counter to how you see the world. But what I argue in I Disagree , and what I really believe in, is starting with listening and understanding when those moments have to happen. And anti-vax is hard, because the health thing is bad there—I made the joke, if you have a newborn baby, that uncle just cannot come to your event and expose the new one to whatever they might be bringing around. But we have really stopped being able to listen to one another. And you will find, actually, when you let people talk, not only do they feel better about the interaction because they were heard—and we’re all desperate for that, frankly—but a lot of times they will tie themselves in knots. They will proverbially hang themselves as they continue down these roads, especially if you are just carefully interjecting little pieces of your reality, and certainly the science. So knowing when to listen, and when to talk. I have something in the book that I call “the soft start”—which if you watch the way that I interact with my colleagues, I use almost all of the time. Which is: Before you get into your point of view, which runs counter to how they’re seeing the world, that you find some kind of connective tissue. This reminder that we are sharing this space with one another, that they matter to us, that you really want to understand their point of view and how they see the world. So an olive branch of some kind. And also humor helps a lot with that. Being able to make a joke or create a moment of levity before you go in with your proverbial haymaker. One of the tips of the book is to think in averages and not in anecdotes. I think back a lot to what Ben Shapiro said when he said, “The facts don’t care about your feelings.” And it kind of became the motto for the Trump era, and this idea of the hysterical liberal that can’t keep it together. And having a background in data and research obviously helps me with this, but making sure that I curate the way that I talk about an issue so that the emphasis is on the trendlines more than it is on the personal stories. And that doesn’t mean that they don’t matter, and I use them regularly. Either something about me—I just had a big back-and-forth a couple months ago with Jesse, with my colleague, about the Save America Act, where I was using the data. But I used my personal story of how hard it was for me to get my Real ID—I had to go to the DMV three times to be able to accomplish that—to make the case that you are going to be disenfranchising voters. And it’s going to be more Republicans than it is Democrats, frankly, when that happens. So those are just some of the techniques that I use in being able to do this. And they work at the table on The Five , and they would also work at a family gathering. But it does require—and not in the Michelle Obama “when they go low we go high” way, because that’s very Pollyanna, and I don’t think that it meets the moment, necessarily—but there is a lot of generosity and kindness that I think needs to be infused in the way that these conversations take place, that will make them much more productive. And, frankly, that we’ll be able to have them after a several years’ hiatus if we do it right. Frum: So I get how this applies to a family situation. That maybe your crazy uncle is in other ways a kindly person, anyway you’re related by blood, and anyway your grandmother cares that he be there, and you care about her. So you indulge the crazy uncle, and we just try to work around him. But outside the familial context, what are we trying to accomplish? When you point out to Jesse Watters the Save America Act will disenfranchise people, if you’re being candid, you say, That’s the point. That’s the point. We want it. Of course, of course—we want to disenfranchise. Now, what I’m worried about is: I am living in a mental world where Republicans had their papers more in order than Democrats did, and that was probably true when George W. Bush and Romney were Republicans. Today, actually, Republicans are messier than Democrats. So the disenfranchisement may backfire. It may not just be minorities; it may be my people too. But when you’re dealing with people who are nonrelatives, what is the reason we try to preserve the conversation rather than get to what is really being talked about? Tarlov: Well, there’s an emotional component, which I was trying to get at with talking about the amount of outreach that I get from people who do want to be having these conversations. People talk a big game about how comfortable they are with their reality, but when you peel back layers, there’s oftentimes a lot of hurt feelings, and a genuine missing that they feel for these people. The second part of it is that there is an underlying level of persuasion, and a different kind of persuasion that can take place. And I make it clear in I Disagree that I don’t see my job as changing minds, but opening them. And I want to go back to the Save America example, because what happened there in Jesse’s reaction was actually a direct extension of being educated about what the bill actually said. It wasn’t a, Oh no, we don’t want this to happen. We don’t want these people to vote. There’s so much misinformation and disinformation about what’s going on in our politics that you need to have these piercing moments to actually break through it. So the right has branded the Save America Act as a voter-ID bill, which is not fair. That is not what this is. It’s a bill where you have to show your birth certificate or a passport to be able to vote. Now, more Democrats than Republicans have passports. The number of people who have their original birth certificate, very few and far between. But you’re looking at people who have changed their names, you’re talking about married women, certainly kids that are away at college and want to be able to vote. They’re not traveling with their birth certificates, et cetera. And so pointing out that the right was being actually pretty craven in saying that this was a voter-ID bill to make it look like we just want to have a bunch of people who are here illegally vote, which is their favorite fraud claim. But instead recentering it on what documents you have to actually show to do, it caused Jesse to question out loud, Oh, is that true? And he does this thing where if Dana Perino confirms it, then he believes me, and she confirmed that that was the case. And he said—I don’t remember the exact words—but like, Oh, that’s messed up. Frum: When you say, Here’s this thing you did that looks pretty immoral, and you did it because you thought it would hurt people you didn’t like. But it turns out, with better information, you realize it hurts people you do like. And then he says, Oh, okay, in that case, I change my mind. What has been achieved? That what you’ve done is—yes, he now has better-informed prejudices. Oh, I didn’t realize that the passport rule was going to hurt my folks. I thought it was going hurt your folks. Now, there’s nothing wrong with having an unsympathetic principal character. Thackeray did it in Vanity Fair. But Becky Sharp, although she’s not a very likable or admirable character, she’s a fascinating character. She’s someone we inhabit from within, and she’s not a completely horrible-in-every-way character. She has certain excellences and attributes, and so do some the people around her. We feel sympathy for her victims, because many of them are nicer people than she is. If you hate everybody and make everybody the butt of your humor and your satire and your polemical points, then we end up living as if we were this unlikable narrator. One of the questions that fans who praise the book will say is, You have to understand; you have to enter into the spirit of the book. And the spirit of the book is “the main character’s nasty, so everybody in the book is nasty”—and that’s the author’s art. But you’re left wondering after a while, maybe it’s not just the characters who are nasty, principal and secondary; maybe the author’s kind of nasty. I’m not sure—I mean, she’s clever, and she’s got funny things to say. I’m not sure I’m enjoying spending time with her and not just with her character. But the book is famous. I’m sure you’ll have a chance to read it for yourself. See if you agree or disagree with me. That’s it for this week’s edition of The David Frum Show. Thanks so much for watching or listening. As always, the best way to support the work of this program is by subscribing to The Atlantic. That way, you get my work and all of my colleagues’. I hope you will consider sharing and promoting the program on whatever social-media platform you use. See you next week here on The David Frum Show. Bye-bye.

items.title: Souveraineté énergétique : le Sénégal prépare une deuxième raffinerie de 4 millions de tonnes
items.description: En marge de la 81e session de l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies, le président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Diakhar Faye, a présidé, mercredi 23 septembre 2026, à New York, la cérémonie de signature d’un protocole d’accord entre la Société africaine de raffinage (SAR) et la compagnie turque Yamata. Cet accord ouvre la voie à un vaste programme visant à renforcer les capacités de raffinage et à accélérer la marche du Sénégal vers la souveraineté énergétique. Le document a été signé par le directeur général de la SAR, Mamadou Abib Diop, et le président-directeur général de Yamata, Cengiz Duyar. Il prévoit notamment la construction d’une deuxième raffinerie d’une capacité de quatre millions de tonnes par an. L’installation sera conçue pour traiter le pétrole brut de Sangomar, mais également une large gamme de bruts disponibles sur le marché international. Un investissement pouvant atteindre 3 milliards de dollars Le coût de cette nouvelle infrastructure est estimé entre 2 et 3 milliards de dollars. Le partenariat prévoit également la modernisation de la raffinerie de Mbao, actuellement en activité, pour un investissement supplémentaire compris entre 300 et 500 millions de dollars. Yamata devra assurer l’ingénierie, les achats, la construction ainsi que le financement du projet. La compagnie turque entend mobiliser les ressources nécessaires auprès de ses partenaires financiers, sans garantie souveraine de l’État du Sénégal. La signature du protocole marque ainsi une nouvelle étape dans le processus. Elle doit permettre de finaliser les études d’ingénierie de détail, présentées comme la dernière phase avant le démarrage de la construction. Couvrir les besoins nationaux et viser le marché régional Depuis le démarrage de sa production pétrolière en 2024, le Sénégal demeure encore largement dépendant des importations de produits pétroliers. La mise en service d’une nouvelle raffinerie doit contribuer à réduire cette dépendance. Selon la présidence de la République, la future installation aura vocation à couvrir l’intégralité des besoins du marché national et à dégager des excédents destinés aux marchés de la sous-région. Le projet s’inscrit ainsi dans une ambition plus large : faire évoluer le Sénégal d’un producteur de pétrole brut vers un pays capable de transformer une partie significative de sa production et de devenir un fournisseur régional de produits raffinés. Des perspectives au-delà du raffinage L’enjeu du projet dépasse toutefois la seule production de carburants. Une capacité de raffinage accrue doit également permettre de fournir des intrants à plusieurs secteurs de l’économie, notamment l’agriculture, les transports, l’industrie et la construction. Le partenariat prévoit par ailleurs le développement de projets connexes dans la pétrochimie. L’objectif est de favoriser la transformation locale des dérivés du pétrole et de faire émerger de nouvelles chaînes de valeur industrielles. La présidence présente ainsi cette initiative comme un projet à effet catalytique, susceptible de stimuler les investissements, le développement des compétences et la participation des entreprises sénégalaises dans plusieurs secteurs. Plus de 15 000 emplois annoncés Le projet devrait générer plus de 15 000 emplois directs durant sa phase de construction, avec une place importante accordée au contenu local. Les métiers liés à l’ingénierie, à la maintenance et à la logistique industrielle figurent notamment parmi les domaines appelés à bénéficier de cette dynamique. À travers ce partenariat, le chef de l’État réaffirme ainsi l’objectif de renforcer la souveraineté énergétique du Sénégal. Pour les autorités, le recours à un financement privé, sans garantie souveraine, doit permettre de porter ce programme d’investissement sans alourdir directement les finances publiques. C.G. DIOP

items.title: Batna : ignoré par ses proches, un jeune marié trouve toute l’Algérie à ses côtés
items.description: L'histoire est triste et merveilleuse à la fois. Triste, parce qu’un jeune orphelin s’est retrouvé presque seul lors de son mariage , ses proches n’ayant pas daigné faire le déplacement. Mais la fin est heureuse. Les habitants de sa ville et de toutes les régions du pays lui ont organisé une fête grandiose. C’est un cas de solidarité collective insolite et émouvant. Laissé seul le jour de son mariage, il reçoit une foule immense L’histoire s’est passée à Merouana, une localité de la wilaya de Batna, dans l’Est de l’Algérie. Salah, un jeune orphelin, a organisé une cérémonie pour son mariage . Seule une poignée de ses amis était présente. Ses proches n’ont pas répondu à l’invitation. Sur une vidéo partagée sur les réseaux sociaux, on voit le jeune homme abattu, dans une salle presque vide. Les plats préparés pour les invités sont restés intacts. Les internautes ont très vite compris ce qu'il s’est passé. Les invités ne sont pas venus parce que le marié est pauvre et orphelin. Ils sont venus de partout pour lui offrir un mariage de rêve Émus, les jeunes de la région se sont donné le mot pour se retrouver chez lui. L'appel à la solidarité est très vite entendu. Les gens sont venus par centaines. Il y avait même des troupes de cavaliers, du baroud, des véhicules de luxe avec des décorations florales, des motos, des mascottes… La place de la ville est noire de monde, les rues et ruelles bloquées par un nombre impressionnant de voitures. « Même les services de sécurité ont été pris de court et ont eu du mal à réguler la circulation avec le grand nombre de véhicules qui a afflué », raconte un témoin dans une autre vidéo sur les réseaux sociaux. « Hier j’étais tout seul, aujourd'hui 69 wilayas sont avec moi » Sur les images, on voit le marié enfin heureux, s'éclatant avec ses « invités » inattendus. Son mariage est passé du plus triste du monde à une fête dont personne ne peut rêver. Il a eu en tout cas « le plus long cortège du monde », selon l’avis des présents. « Hier j’étais tout seul, aujourd'hui toute l’Algérie, 69 wilayas sont avec moi », déclare Salah. Les gens sont, en effet, venus de Merouana, d’autres localités de Batna et de nombreuses wilayas du pays. Cette histoire fera date. Elle illustre la solidarité séculaire des Algériens. L’article Batna : ignoré par ses proches, un jeune marié trouve toute l’Algérie à ses côtés est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Wael Naouar annonce la suspension de sa grève de la faim après 38 jours
items.description: Wael Naouar a annoncé, dans la soirée de ce mercredi 23 septembre 2026, la suspension de sa grève de la faim après 38 jours d'action protestataire contre son arrestation et celle de ses camarades de la flotille Al-Soumoud. Dans un message adressé à l'opinion publique, l'activiste qui est en détention, explique avoir pris cette décision en réponse aux demandes pressantes de sa famille et de son comité de défense, inquiets de la dégradation critique de son état de santé, ainsi qu'aux appels lancés par diverses organisations nationales, forces politiques et activistes de la société civile. Dans son message, il a adressé un hommage particulier à l'avocat Ayachi Hammami pour son geste de solidarité mené depuis sa cellule, tout en exprimant sa gratitude envers ses proches et l'ensemble de ses soutiens. Par la même occasion, il a appelé ses camarades de la flotille Al-Soumoud arrêtés avec lui, à savoir Ghassen Henchiri, Ghassen Boghdiri et Nabil Chennoufi, à mettre fin eux aussi à leur grève de la faim afin de préserver leur santé et de poursuivre le combat sous d'autres formes. Wael Wael Naouar a par ailleurs souligné que la suspension de ce mouvement de protestation ne constitue en rien un renoncement à ses revendications ou à sa lutte pour la liberté. Y. N. L’article Wael Naouar annonce la suspension de sa grève de la faim après 38 jours est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Kaolack : Le FSDT installe sa structure départementale et annonce 72 heures de grève
items.description: Le Front syndical pour la défense du travail (FSDT) a installé, ce mercredi 23 septembre 2026, a structure départementale à Kaolack. La cérémonie, tenue à la Chambre des métiers, a été mise à profit pour informer les organisations membres sur le nouveau Code du travail, le Pacte de stabilité sociale et le plan d’action réactualisé du mouvement syndical. La rencontre a réuni plusieurs organisations autour des questions d’emploi, de conditions de travail, de protection sociale et de dialogue avec les pouvoirs publics. En marge de la cérémonie, le secrétaire général de la CNTS, Mody Guiro, a invité le ministre de tutelle à privilégier la concertation. « On n’a rien contre le ministre de tutelle lui-même. Mais, à partir de sa fonction, il crée la zizanie. Il l’a même dit : “je vais mettre de l’ordre” », a-t-il déclaré. Estimant que « le dialogue social doit demeurer au cœur » des relations entre autorités et syndicats, Mody Guiro a dénoncé un discours qu’il juge incompatible avec l’esprit de concertation. Dans ce contexte, le FSDT annonce une grève générale de 72 heures, les 21, 22 et 23 octobre 2026, dans les secteurs public, privé et informel. Le mouvement réclame notamment la révision du CDD de quatre ans, l’amélioration de la gouvernance de l’IPRES et de la CSS, l’application de la Convention n°144 de l’OIT, la réintégration de travailleurs licenciés et l’amélioration des conditions salariales et sociales. À Kaolack, le Front entend renforcer son implantation et préparer cette mobilisation prévue en octobre prochain. Mamadou THIAM ( Correspondant)

items.title: Nations unies : « L’Afrique doit être à la table, pas au menu » (Antonio Guterres)
items.description: L’Afrique doit obtenir une place permanente au conseil de sécurité des Nations unies. C’est l’appel lancé par le secrétaire général de l’ONU, Antonio Guterres, lors de l’ouverture du débat général de la 81ᵉ session de l’Assemblée générale, le 22 septembre 2026 à New York. Selon le secrétaire général de l’ONU, António Guterres, l’absence de représentation permanente africaine ne correspond plus aux réalités géopolitiques actuelles. « L’Afrique doit être à la table, pas au menu », a-t-il déclaré, appelant les États membres à rendre le conseil de sécurité plus représentatif et plus légitime. L’Afrique ne dispose actuellement d’aucun siège permanent, alors même que le continent est directement concerné par plusieurs dossiers majeurs traités par le conseil, notamment les questions de paix et de sécurité. Pour rappel, le conseil compte actuellement 15 membres, dont cinq permanents disposant du droit de veto : les États-Unis, la Russie, la Chine, la France et le Royaume-Uni. Minute.bf

items.title: A l’ONU, le Burkina appelle à la fin des inégalités et à une réforme de l’architecture financière internationale
items.description: (New-York, le 23 septembre 2026) Les travaux de la 81e Assemblée générale des Nations Unies se sont poursuivis ce 23 septembre avec plusieurs réunions de haut niveau, dont celle relative à la commémoration du 40e anniversaire de la Déclaration des Nations Unies de 1986 sur le droit au développement. Le ministre des Affaires étrangères qui a livré la déclaration du Burkina Faso à cette occasion, a salué la tenue de cet évènement tout en déplorant la persistance de profondes inégalités entre les nations et au sein des sociétés. Devant l'assistance, il a présenté la vision du Burkina Faso sur le développement, qui doit reposer sur la liberté de définir sa propre voie pour un développement endogène, souverain et durable, à travers une production et une transformation locales des ressources, ainsi qu'un renforcement des capacités nationales. Il a présenté les résultats encourageants obtenus par le Burkina Faso grâce à cette vision et malgré les défis sécuritaires. >, a t-il déclaré. Le Chef de la diplomatie burkinabè a par ailleurs indiqué que les pays de la Confédération des États du Sahel assument pleinement leur responsabilité de protéger leurs peuples et leurs territoires. >, a martelé le Camarade ministre Karamoko Jean Marie TRAORE. Pour lui, lorsque les mécanismes de justice internationale sont dévoyés et utilisés comme des instruments de pression politique, leur crédibilité s’en trouve profondément affectée, et c'est dans ce contexte que les États membres de la Confédération des États du Sahel ont engagé leur retrait du Statut de Rome de la Cour pénale internationale. Pour terminer, il a souligné l’exigence d’une réforme de l’architecture financière internationale, d'une fiscalité plus équitable et le renforcement des capacités productives nationales, pour la réalisation du droit au développement. Cette réalisation exige également que le terrorisme, les ingérences ainsi que les atteintes à la souveraineté et à l’intégrité territoriale soient reconnus comme des entraves au développement. >, a conclu le ministre des Affaires étrangères. DCRP/MAE L’article A l'ONU, le Burkina appelle à la fin des inégalités et à une réforme de l’architecture financière internationale est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

Alioune Abitalib Fall succède à Mame Moussa Cissé à la tête des Lionnes, mettant fin au cycle entamé par ce dernier, qui avait conduit l'équipe à trois qualifications consécutives à la Coupe d'Afrique des nations et à deux quarts de finale successifs (2022, 2024). Ancien entraîneur des U20 féminines, Alioune Abitalib Fall connaît bien le vivier de jeunes talentueuses appelées à intégrer, à terme, la sélection A. Sa nomination s'inscrit dans une volonté de continuité générationnelle, alors que le Sénégal ambitionne toujours de décrocher une première qualification pour la Coupe du monde féminine. Le nouveau technicien hérite d'un groupe compétitif, marqué par une présence croissante de joueuses expatriées évoluant dans des championnats européens, aux côtés d'un socle local structuré autour des Aigles de la Médina. Sa mission : consolider les acquis et franchir un nouveau palier lors des prochaines échéances continentales. C.G.D

items.title: International U17: Souleymane « Commissaire » Faye à Chelsea pour des tests
items.description: Le jeune international sénégalais Souleymane « Commissaire » Faye se trouve actuellement à Londres pour effectuer une série de tests à Chelsea, selon wiwsport. Âgé de 16 ans, le milieu offensif de Be Sport Academy a rejoint l’Angleterre après la finale du tournoi UFOA-A U17. Cette nouvelle expérience vient récompenser une progression remarquée au sein des sélections de jeunes du Sénégal. En 2025, Faye avait été élu meilleur joueur et meilleur buteur du tournoi UFOA-A U17, remporté par les Lionceaux à Bamako. Il s’était également distingué avec la sélection scolaire U15, sacrée championne, en décrochant les mêmes distinctions individuelles. Le jeune talent a confirmé en 2026 lors de la CAN U17 au Maroc, remportée par le Sénégal. Il a ensuite participé au tournoi UFOA-A organisé au Sénégal, avec trois buts à son actif, malgré la défaite des Lionceaux en finale face à la Gambie aux tirs au but (3-5). Courtisé par plusieurs clubs européens, Souleymane Faye attire notamment par son profil offensif, qui lui vaut parfois d’être comparé à Cole Palmer. Aucune signature n’est toutefois annoncée à ce stade. Son séjour à Chelsea doit d’abord lui permettre de passer des tests et de découvrir l’environnement du club londonien. C.G.D

items.title: El símbolo de un derecho roto
items.description: Maricarmen Abascal tenía 17 años cuando, en 1956, entró por primera vez en el piso que alquilaron sus padres en la calle Sainz de Baranda, en Madrid. Ha vivido en él toda su vida y en él esperaba pasar su vejez. Este miércoles, a los 87 años de edad, con problemas de movilidad y sin alternativa habitacional, fue obligada por una orden judicial a salir de su casa para no volver jamás. Maricarmen fue desahuciada en medio de un potente despliegue policial, en camilla, con cientos de personas en la calle gritando: “¡No estás sola!”. Toda la escena fue retransmitida en directo por los medios y las redes a un país con el corazón en un puño, porque el trauma personal de esta anciana madrileña conecta con un país que desde hace años sufre la vivienda como un drama. items.title: Six Hard-to-Find Books Worth Reading
items.description: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. Many enthusiastic readers have a personal canon—a unique collection of books they return to for pleasure, edification, or escape. These lists almost always contain works of popular distinction, works so incredible (and so incredibly well-known) that their inclusion surprises no one. But these private lists also tend to include novels that few other people know well, or at all. The sheer volume of printed matter means that a book that once rightfully inspired devotion can simply fall out of favor, or even out of print—but for its loyal fans, a work’s obscurity might actually increase its private value. Below are six books that I believe are unfairly unheralded. These titles are no longer fashionable, if they ever were. They largely exist outside today’s literary conversation. Some have been rescued and reprinted by indie presses; some can be found only in used-book stores or on niche websites. But should you manage to read one of these selections, you’ll be treated to formal complexity and artistic delight that might just make them permanent additions to your own collection. Solo Faces , by James Salter Implying that Salter is neglected, let alone forgotten, would be silly: Both his gorgeous, accomplished novel Light Years and the lyrically erotic A Sport and a Pastime remain touchstones. But I think that the brilliance of these two works has crowded out other masterful efforts, including Solo Faces . This novel follows Vernon Rand, a mountaineer and wanderer whose obsession with the climb alienates him from the more quotidian aspects of his life. The result is a lean, flinty story about a modern-day outlaw, a desperate and strangely pure loner ever at odds with the world. The greatness of Solo Faces is that Salter tests himself as much as Rand does. His rhetorical control captures and ennobles climactic mountain rescues and interpersonal struggles alike. This sophisticated work would get my vote as the greatest sporting novel ever written—and thankfully, it’s still in print from North Point Press. Passacaglia , by Robert Pinget Passacaglia is my favorite book to come out of the nouveau roman, a movement whose writers tore down novelistic architecture—plot, chronology, linear narration—in order to explore new creative possibilities. In this case, Pinget marshals spare language and opaque storylines to memorable effect, making thrilling demands of readers willing to enter his puzzle box. The book follows a man known as The Master, who spends most of his time meditating on the recent death of “an idiot” who had lived with him. As he turns over memories, talks with the local doctor, and writes in his notebooks, the death takes on an uncertain, dreamlike quality that will remain with you long after you finish reading the novel. Passacaglia remains sadly out of print in English, though its laconic chill makes it more than worth tracking down. [ Read: Six cult classics you have to read ] Yesterday’s Burdens , by Robert M. Coates If Coates survives in historical memory, it’s as a Lost Generation footnote—the man who first introduced Ernest Hemingway to Gertrude Stein. This is an unfortunate legacy, though, for an audacious American literary experimenter whose 1926 debut, The Eater of Darkness , was called “the first Dada novel in English.” Because Coates worked for three decades as The New Yorker ’s art critic, something of a painter’s visual language is found in his strange, oblique sentences. My favorite of his novels is Yesterday’s Burdens , of which Stein was an admirer. (“It is so exciting because it is modern,” she declared.) The novel follows the restless Henderson, a young man who wanders Manhattan, visiting speakeasies and crashing parties to keep despair at bay. Coates absorbs the city’s fabulous energies and arranges the tumult into rich, cubist sketches that reproduce overlapping advertising slogans, subway signs, motor cars, and overheard conversations. After being out of print for decades, Yesterday’s Burdens was resurrected in 2020 by Tough Poets Press. Rife with formal oddities and stylistic verve, this masterpiece captures New York in language that still feels fresh nearly a century later. The Crazy Hunter , by Kay Boyle Like Coates, Boyle was known, mostly against her will, as a member of the Lost Generation. She also shares with Coates the fate of falling from fashion. Her 14 compact, psychologically percipient novels have been unjustly overlooked for the past half century. Each is a bit like a short story given room to run: They possess that form’s suggestive, poetic compression and intensity. At just about 140 pages, The Crazy Hunter is archetypal. It is a story of English country life in which a girl fights to save a magnificent blind horse, even though her domineering mother has determined that the animal should be put down. The novel never gives in to the temptation of melodrama, offering instead a restrained moral subtlety. Not as flashy as other modernists, Boyle is perhaps easier to dismiss—but Pushkin Press’s 2024 reissue means you can try her bristling vignettes, where you’ll find that Boyle deserves to be read alongside the other American greats of her time. [ Read: Read these six books—just trust us ] With My Dog-Eyes , by Hilda Hilst Hilst wrote novels that convulse with madness, death, and obscenity. Her works, short and confounding, unfurl like oppressive dreams. A certain comfort with disorientation is necessary to read her fruitfully. This is true of With My Dog-Eyes , which follows the unraveling of Amós Kéres, a mathematics professor, whose lengthy and inexplicable silences during lectures have prompted the dean to place him on administrative leave. From the first page, Hilst depicts Kéres’s psychic fissures with a range of unfamiliar narrative choices: changes of tense, first-to-third-person jumps, streams of consciousness, and baffling leaps in time and circumstance. The world may look different to you after you’ve read Hilst. Although many of her novels have sadly gone out of print, With My Dog-Eyes remains available by way of Melville House. Lookout Cartridge , by Joseph McElroy McElroy, at a sprightly 96, is the last titan of a particularly rich era in American fiction. He’s probably best known for his towering Women & Men , a more-than-1,000-page opus that analyzes and rhapsodizes 1970s New York City. It’s a great novel; however, in my experience, Lookout Cartridge is the McElroy fan’s favorite McElroy. Cartwright and Dagger, two Americans in England, have been shooting an experimental film, a kind of meta-montage of late-20th-century life that exudes wary mysticism. Someone has exposed the film to the sun, thus destroying it. (Or so Dagger tells Cartwright.) An obsessive mystery unfolds around the film’s destruction, in which classic tropes from the detective novel are also irradiated and discarded. Answers are rarely forthcoming, and often evidence is merely another opportunity for obfuscation. The novel’s protagonists are trapped within the sinister triangulation of powers they cannot understand. Currently out of print, a physical copy of Lookout Cartridge is well worth a search at your local used-book store.

items.title: Inclusion des personnes handicapées : Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba Mbacké de l’Open Society Senegal appelle à un cadre juridique pour l’accessibilité numérique
items.description: L’accès aux services numériques reste un défi pour les personnes en situation de handicap. Pour Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba Mbacké, de l’ISOC Sénégal, les données relatives à l’accès à l’emploi, aux services numériques publics et à l’accessibilité des plateformes en ligne ne permettent pas « une égale dignité de l’application du numérique ». « Même si les gens ne s’entendent pas totalement sur les chiffres, on estime qu’il y a 1,7 million de personnes vivant avec un handicap. Parmi elles, 800 000 seraient en âge de travailler, mais ne seraient pas en position d’avoir un accès à l’emploi et 12 % des personnes en situation de handicap déclareraient utiliser régulièrement un service numérique public », précise-t-il. Dans ce sillage, un rapport du WCAG, l’organisme chargé de la normalisation des plateformes numériques en matière d’accessibilité, évalue que 15 % de la population mondiale vivrait avec un handicap, tandis que 98 % des sites web publics mondiaux ne respecteraient pas les standards d’accessibilité, souligne-t-il. Pour Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba Mbacké, cette situation est aggravée par l’absence de politiques publiques permettant d’inclure les personnes en situation de handicap. « Malgré ces chiffres, il n’y a pas encore de politique claire qui permette d’inclure ces personnes qui ont un handicap », affirme-t-il. De même, il regrette que le Sénégal, qui est signataire depuis 2007 de la Convention des Nations unies relative aux droits des personnes handicapées, ne respecte pas ces conventions. Une feuille de route avec tous les acteurs Dans ce sillage, afin de mieux inclure cette partie de la population dans les politiques numériques, le président d’ISOC Sénégal préconise l’implication de tous les acteurs dans le but de mettre en place une feuille de route applicable. « Nous avons besoin des experts du domaine, des personnes handicapées ainsi que des responsables politiques et administratifs. Il faut qu’à l’aide de toutes ces personnes, on mette en place une feuille de route qui soit utilisable par les institutions, qui donne les directives », indique-t-il. Face à cette situation, l’enseignant-chercheur à l’ESP plaide pour l’élaboration de directives et la mise en place d’un cadre permettant de renforcer l’accessibilité numérique. « On a besoin que ces différentes règles passent même à l’Assemblée nationale, qu’elles fassent l’objet de lois. On a aussi besoin d’un cercle de discussion où ces différentes directives vont pouvoir être mises en place », déclare-t-il. Marème Fatou Dramé

items.title: Section 144 imposed in Islamabad; district admin warns citizens against participating in any 'illegal activity'
items.description: Section 144 has been imposed for two months in Islamabad, it emerged on Wednesday, with the district administration warning citizens against participating in any “illegal activity”. The order comes as the Kissan Ittehad and PTI have announced long marches and sit-ins in Islamabad in the coming week. The PTI has announced a long march on Sept 27 to press for the release of its founder, Imran Khan, who is currently incarcerated in Rawalpindi’s Adiala jail. A copy of the order, issued by Islamabad Additional District Magistrate Dr Anam Fatima and dated Sept 18, is available with Dawn . According to the order, Section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code has been enforced with immediate effect and “shall remain in force for a period of two months”. The order prohibited gatherings of five or more people, as well as processions, rallies and demonstrations, at any public place within the revenue limits of the district, including the Red Zone. Highlighting that “certain segments of society” were planning to organise “unlawful assemblies”, the order termed it “necessary to control such types of illegal activities which present a threat to public peace, tranquillity and maintenance of law and order”. It added that processions and demonstrations being planned in the territory were likely to threaten public peace, cause annoyance and injury, endanger human life and safety, threaten public property and could lead to a riot in Islamabad. On these grounds, it stated that “immediate prevention and speedy remedy is required” to protect life and property. In a separate statement issued on Wednesday, the district administration said that Section 144 had been enforced in the federal capital. “No gatherings or assemblies of any kind are permitted in the city. Gatherings are also banned under the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act 2024,” the district administration said. It said that strict legal action will be taken in the event of a violation, adding that violation of the act carried a penalty of three years’ imprisonment. “Citizens are urged not to participate in any illegal activity, and to cooperate with security agencies and demonstrate responsibility,” it added. Preparations in the Rawalpindi Division and the federal capital territory to maintain security and deal with any emergency situation are in full swing in light of the potential long march by the PTI and other protests in Islamabad. Section 144 has also separately been enforced across Punjab for 13 days, in view of “serious threats” to public peace, tranquillity, and the lives and property of citizens across Punjab. The Punjab government has also requested the federal government to deploy Rangers in Rawalpindi, Attock, Jhelum and Mianwali districts from Sept 22 to Oct 5 to assist the provincial police in maintaining law and order amid the expected protest on Sept 27. In August, the federal government authorised the deployment of three companies of the Pakistan Army in Rawalpindi for six months to perform “sensitive security duties” and respond to any unforeseen situation.

items.title: 40e anniversaire de l’agression terroriste du 23 septembre 1986 : Une gerbe déposée en mémoire des victimes à Lomé
items.description: Lomé, 23 sept. (ATOP) – Le président de l’Assemblée nationale, Prof Komi Selom Klassou, représentant le Président du Conseil, a déposé, le mercredi 23 septembre, à la Place des Martyrs à Lomé, une gerbe de fleurs en hommage aux victimes de l’agression terroriste du 23 septembre 1986. Les officiels Après le dépôt de gerbe de fleurs, le président de l’Assemblée nationale a observé une minute de silence dans le recueillement, suivi de la sonnerie aux morts des Forces armées togolaises, et l’exécution de l’hymne national, « Terre de nos aïeux ». L’ambiance était entretenue par la chorale des femmes. Ce geste de mémoire s’inscrit dans le cadre de la commémoration du 40 e anniversaire de cette attaque. La cérémonie a réuni des représentants des institutions de la République, des officiers supérieurs des Forces armées togolaises (FAT), ainsi que des autorités administratives et coutumières. L’agression du 23 septembre 1986 avait été menée par un groupe armé venu de l’extérieur du territoire national. Les assaillants avaient pris pour cible plusieurs points stratégiques de Lomé dans la nuit du 23 au 24 septembre, faisant des victimes parmi les forces de défense et de sécurité et les populations civiles. ATOP/IS/AO

items.title: Govt reduces petrol price by Rs1.93 per litre, HSD by Rs4.21 per litre
items.description: Pakistan fuel prices, 2026 Official ex-depot prices (PKR/litre) — OGRA & Ministry of Energy notifications Petrol (MS-92) Diesel (HSD) Pre-crisis baseline Source: OGRA / Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division); Dawn.com · "> The government on Wednesday reduced the price of petrol by Rs1.93 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs4.21 per litre. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs390.12 per litre while HSD will cost Rs414.75 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will be applicable for Sept 24 (Thursday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Abrar Ahmed rises to No. 1 in ICC T20I bowling rankings
items.description: Pakistan’s Abrar Ahmed has risen to the top of the ICC Men’s T20I bowling rankings for the first time in his career, ending Afghanistan leg-spinner Rashid Khan’s six-month reign at No. 1. Abrar moved to the summit after Rashid slipped one rating point behind the Pakistan spinner’s tally of 736 following an unimpressive outing against India. The 28-year-old became only the fifth Pakistan bowler to top the T20I bowling rankings, following Umar Gul, Saeed Ajmal, Imad Wasim and Shahid Afridi. Abrar, who has played 10 Tests, 19 ODIs and 38 T20Is for Pakistan, has taken 133 international wickets. He is also ranked second in the ODI bowling rankings, 39 rating points behind Rashid, who occupies the top position in that format. The Karachi-born right-arm mystery spinner has featured in nine T20Is for Pakistan this year and taken 15 wickets, including six in the three-match home series against Australia, which Pakistan won 3-0 in January and February. Abrar said the achievement fulfilled a long-held ambition of his. “When you start playing cricket, you have only one dream to represent Pakistan. Once you achieve that, the next dream is to become world number one,” he was quoted as saying by the Pakistan Cricket Board’s digital platform. “I feel very proud to become the world number one bowler while representing Pakistan. I will continue working hard to achieve more success and win more matches for Pakistan.” Abrar said improving his consistency had been a particular focus of his work. “In the past, I had variations in my bowling, but consistency was an area I needed to improve. I worked hard on my consistency and that work has helped me improve a lot,” he said. He is currently with Pakistan’s Asian Games squad, which is undergoing a four-day training camp in Karachi ahead of the competition in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. “My aim is to perform well and help my team win matches and return to Pakistan with a gold medal,” Abrar said.

items.title: Mouhamed Ali Ndiaye, boxeur: une vie en Italie après les rings
items.description: Certains sportifs ont marqué l’arène par leurs exploits avant de se réinventer ou de se reconvertir après leur carrière sportive. La rubrique « Que sont-ils devenus ? » raconte leur vie d’après-carrière. Aujourd’hui, coup de projecteur sur le boxeur Mouhamed Ali Ndiaye. Il a connu une trajectoire singulière entre Pikine, la France et l’Italie. Son père, Moussa Ndiaye, ancien boxeur du club des Niayes de Pikine depuis 1967, était un fervent admirateur du grand champion américain Mouhamed Ali. Il suivait avec passion les exploits de celui qu’il considérait comme un modèle pour son style, son courage, son sang-froid et son éloquence. C’est donc tout naturellement qu’il donne à son fils le prénom de son idole. Le hasard fera ensuite le reste. En effet, lorsque la légende américaine séjourne au Sénégal, la famille Ndiaye réussit à établir un contact avec lui. Le jeune Mouhamed Ali garde de ces rencontres un souvenir particulier. « Mouhamed Ali est venu au Sénégal pour la toute première fois en février 1980. J’étais né et j’avais juste cinq mois. On m’a raconté qu’a mes cinq mois, on me l’a présenté », dit-il. Dix ans plus tard, alors qu’il est encore enfant, il a de nouveau l’occasion de croiser la route de son célèbre homonyme lors de son second passage au Sénégal. Le nom, finalement, aura accompagné toute sa vie. À seulement 12 ans, il dispute son premier combat en 1991, lors de la première édition du Mémorial Battling Siki, au stade Marius Ndiaye. Dans cet environnement où il apprend progressivement les rudiments du noble art, il bénéficie des conseils de Joseph Diouf, Antoine Marème Mbengue et Alex Tavarez. Le jeune boxeur progresse rapidement. Des années plus tard, il allait se construire une réputation sur les rings. De Pikine à Pontedera en Italie « J’ai débuté dans une école de boxe. Mon père a été mon premier formateur, mon premier pilier », raconte-t-il. Entre 1997 et 1999, il s’adjuge à trois reprises le titre de champion du Sénégal. Trois couronnes nationales qui confortent ses ambitions et lui ouvrent les portes de l’équipe nationale. En 2000, il participe aux compétitions qualificatives pour les Jeux olympiques de Sydney, en Égypte, avec la sélection sénégalaise. Il partage alors l’aventure avec Pape Mamadou Sow et Laurent Gomis. Mais cette campagne olympique ne lui permet pas d’atteindre son objectif. « Par la suite, j’ai concouru pour la qualification aux Jeux olympiques de Sydney en 2000, en Égypte, avec l’équipe nationale. J’étais avec Pape Mamadou Sow et Laurent Gomis. Après cette compétition, nous étions rentrés au Sénégal », se souvient-il. Cette période marque pourtant un déclic. Le Sénégal commence à devenir trop étroit pour ses ambitions. Mouhamed Ali Ndiaye veut aller voir ailleurs, découvrir d’autres méthodes et surtout trouver les conditions nécessaires pour poursuivre sa carrière. Il décide alors de tenter l’aventure européenne. En 2000, Mouhamed Ali Ndiaye quitte le Sénégal. Son premier point de chute est la France, où il reste quelques mois. Mais c’est finalement l’Italie qui va devenir sa seconde patrie. Il s’installe à Pontedera, dans la province de Pise, en Toscane. Le rêve de carrière sportive se heurte toutefois aux réalités de l’immigration. Pendant deux ans, il vit sans titre de séjour et doit multiplier les petits métiers pour subvenir à ses besoins. « C’est à partir de là que j’ai décidé d’aller en Europe en 2000. J’étais d’abord allé en France, où j’ai séjourné quelques mois, avant de migrer vers l’Italie. Pendant deux années, je n’avais pas de papiers administratifs », explique-t-il. Cette période difficile aurait pu mettre fin à ses ambitions. Mais le Sénégalais s’accroche. Il veut retrouver les rings. En 2002, une fois sa situation administrative régularisée, il reprend la boxe amateur en Italie. Le chemin est long, mais sa détermination finit par payer. Ses performances lui permettent d’intégrer la sélection italienne. L’Institut culturel italien de Dakar présente d’ailleurs son parcours comme celui d’un boxeur italo-sénégalais devenu champion d’Italie et champion d’Europe des super-moyens. En 2004, il devient champion d’Italie. Une performance historique dans son parcours et un premier grand accomplissement dans son pays d’adoption. Il passe ensuite professionnel le 1er octobre 2005. Pour ses débuts chez les professionnels, il s’impose par K.-O. face au Ghanéen Thomas Dodoo. Le jeune homme de Pikine, parti quelques années plus tôt à la recherche d’un avenir meilleur, commence alors à se faire un nom sur la scène pugilistique italienne. Après avoir conquis l’Italie, Mouhamed Ali Ndiaye s’attaque aux titres européens. Il remporte le championnat de l’Union européenne en 2011 chez les super-moyens et défend sa ceinture l’année suivante. Cette réussite vient couronner plusieurs années de sacrifices. Mais, pour lui, le chemin parcouru compte presque autant que les titres. Un souvenir reste particulièrement fort : celui de sa rencontre avec le Président Abdoulaye Wade, au Palais de la République. « Ma rencontre avec le Président Abdoulaye Wade, c’était en 2008, quand j’ai remporté le titre du championnat d’Italie. Je fus le premier champion d’Italie venant du Sénégal. C’était lorsque Bacar Dia était ministre des Sports du Sénégal. Le Président Wade avait envoyé une délégation venue du Sénégal pour me soutenir. Quand j’ai gagné le titre, je suis revenu au Sénégal et le Président Wade m’avait reçu au Palais », raconte-t-il. Le Président Wade lui avait alors rendu hommage en le présentant comme « un exemple pour la jeunesse sénégalaise, un modèle de courage ». À cette époque, se souvient-il, la boxe sénégalaise traversait pourtant une période compliquée. La sélection nationale n’avait pas réussi à franchir certaines étapes qualificatives et le pays manquait plusieurs grands rendez-vous internationaux. Mouhamed Ali Ndiaye mesure alors le chemin parcouru. Quelques années auparavant, il combattait encore au Sénégal. Désormais, il porte les couleurs de l’Italie et s’impose sur les rings européens. Place à la solidarité Après plus d’une décennie consacrée à la boxe de haut niveau, Mouhamed Ali Ndiaye finit par tourner la page du ring. Des problèmes de santé aux yeux l’obligent à ralentir, puis à mettre un terme à sa carrière professionnelle. « J’ai arrêté la pratique de la boxe professionnelle en 2015-2016 à cause d’un problème aux yeux », confie-t-il. Pour beaucoup de sportifs, la fin d’une carrière peut ressembler à un vide. Pour Mouhamed Ali Ndiaye, elle devient plutôt le début d’un nouveau combat. Il se tourne vers le social et le bénévolat. En Italie, il s’engage notamment auprès de la Croix-Rouge italienne et devient volontaire chez les sapeurs-pompiers. Son parcours dans le monde associatif lui permet de mettre son expérience et sa notoriété au service des autres. Il vit toujours à Pontedera, où il s’est installé avec sa famille. Son engagement en faveur des personnes handicapées prend également une dimension internationale. En 2012, il est nommé ambassadeur de bonne volonté pour les personnes handicapées. Il s’investit notamment dans des actions destinées à faciliter leur mobilité au Sénégal. L’Institut culturel italien rappelle son engagement pour l’acheminement de moyens destinés aux personnes handicapées à Pikine ainsi que son implication dans l’envoi d’ambulances et de véhicules de secours vers le Sénégal. Il s’engage désormais pour apporter du secours, accompagner les plus vulnérables et créer des passerelles entre l’Italie et le Sénégal. Son parcours attire également l’attention dans son pays d’adoption. En 2019, son histoire est racontée dans un ouvrage écrit avec la journaliste et écrivaine italienne Rita Coruzzi. Intitulé « Mi chiamo Mouhamed Ali », le livre retrace son parcours, de son enfance au Sénégal à son installation en Italie, en passant par les difficultés rencontrées avant sa réussite sportive. En 2021, l’Institut culturel italien de Dakar lui consacre une rencontre autour de cet ouvrage. « Je souhaite venir au Sénégal pour rencontrer le président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, et lui présenter mon livre », dit-il. À Pontedera, il est devenu un visage connu. Au Sénégal, son nom reste associé à une génération de boxeurs qui ont porté haut les couleurs nationales. Par Abdoulaye DEMBÉLÉ
